Centrifugal pump basics

A centrifugal pump moves fluid by turning the kinetic energy of a spinning impeller into pressure. The fluid enters at the eye of the impeller and is thrown outward by the vanes, so the casing sees a higher pressure than the inlet.[1]

Reading a pump curve

The pump curve plots head against flow rate for a fixed impeller diameter and speed. As the flow rate rises the head falls, and the point where the system curve crosses the pump curve is the operating point. Trimming the impeller shifts the whole curve downward, which is why a smaller diameter delivers less flow at the same head.

Efficiency peaks near the best efficiency point. Running far to the left of that point causes recirculation inside the casing, and running far to the right risks cavitation at the inlet. Operators therefore try to keep the operating point within about ten percent of the best efficiency flow.

Net positive suction head

Cavitation begins when the pressure at the impeller eye drops below the vapor pressure of the liquid. The margin between the available suction pressure and that limit is called the net positive suction head, and the pump maker publishes the required value for every model. A designer must make sure that the available value exceeds the required one by a comfortable margin.

Two useful rules follow from this. First, keep the suction line short and straight, because every fitting adds loss. Second, never throttle the suction valve to control flow, because that lowers the available head exactly where it is needed.
